column1: Is this new story proof in physics that MOND is finished? Https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/is-dark-matter-s-main-rival-theory-dead-the-cassini-spacecraft-and-other-recent-tests-may-invalidate-mond/ar-BB1maqMN?ocid=hpmsn&cvid=31541f6e52e74450 I've read the article. It does seem that the latest data from the Cassini spacecraft has delivered another blow to Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND), a theory that attempts to explain the observed rotation curves of galaxies without resorting to dark matter. The article also summarizes some recent developments that push MOND into a corner, which is not to say it’s “finished”. It’s just that the number of observations that are incompatible with MOND keeps growing at an alarming rate. And no, it’s not "proof"; in science, there is no such thing, and the headline is clickbait. Science is always a work in progress, and theories are constantly being refined or even replaced in light of new evidence. The standard model of particle physics itself, the most experimentally corroborated theory in the history of science, keeps being challenged by ever more precise experiments. But you know, what’s truly remarkable is this: The very fact that such a radical idea as MOND could even be entertained, let alone gain any traction in the astronomical community, tells you something deep about the mysteries of dark matter, which no one has ever seen, and dark energy, which no one has ever directly measured or touched. The vast majority of the Universe is this stuff that we can’t possibly even *see* and yet somehow, it is what determines the evolution of the universe and our place in it. Is the force of gravity instantaneous, or does it take time? There is no such thing as the “force of gravity.” That’s just a figure of speech, shorthand for a specific arrangement of spacetime. In general relativity, gravity is not a force; it’s the curvature of spacetime caused by the presence of mass and energy. Think of a bowling ball placed in the center of a trampoline, causing the surface to dip. Now, roll a marble across the trampoline. Its path curves towards the bowling ball, not because of some magical "force," but because it follows the curvature of the trampoline’s surface. So, in that sense, gravity propagates at the speed of light. If you were to, hypothetically, instantly remove the bowling ball, the trampoline’s deformation would change, and the marble would be rerouted on its new trajectory. Gravitational waves carry this information at the speed of light, which is the maximum speed at which any information regarding the presence of mass can travel. The time it takes for gravity to "act" is, therefore, the time it takes for this information to be conveyed. Mind you, this is all a simplified picture. What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? Yes, it's a bit of a loaded question, isn't it? Particularly because the very word "observation" is a shifty one with different meanings depending on context. But let’s crack it out. In the double-slit experiment, the crucial element is *measuring* which slit the photon goes through. It doesn’t necessarily involve the visual apparatus of an intelligent creature; the fundamental issue is *detecting* the photon’s trajectory. When a detector is specifically set up to ascertain which slit the photon traversed, the interference pattern disappears, and the photon behaves as a particle. But if no such measurement is made, the photon goes through *both* slits simultaneously, and the interference pattern becomes apparent, thus behaving as a wave. So, a simple answer to your question is: observation, in this context, is equivalent to measurement of the photon's path. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Could gravitational redshift account for all cosmological redshift? If it includes all the matter inside the sphere between source and observer (radius)? The answer is straightforward: No. Gravitational redshift and cosmological redshift, while both related to the phenomenon of light losing energy, are fundamentally different. Gravitational redshift is a local effect, arising from the gravitational potential difference between the emitter and the receiver of a photon. It is path-dependent; the redshift experienced by the photon depends on every detail of its trajectory through the gravitational field. Thus, to calculate gravitational redshift, one must painstakingly trace the photon’s path from the source to the observer and accumulate the infinitesimal changes in the photon’s energy along each step. Cosmological redshift, instead, is a global effect, caused by the expansion of the universe, and it is in no way related to any gravitational field. It is path-independent: The redshift experienced by the photon depends exclusively on the difference of the scale factor at the time it was emitted vs. the moment it was received. It is a feature of empty space, as it expands, and, to that degree, as space expands, every photon that has ever traveled in it, is subject to it. So even in the special case where both the emitter and the receiver are located inside a static, non-expanding, spherically symmetric distribution of matter (such as a galaxy or galaxy cluster), the cosmological redshift would be zero. Only the gravitational redshift would be non-zero. Indeed, the gravitational redshift can be either positive or negative and depends on the position of the emitter.
